mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly defines equal sets?

options.A: Two sets are equal if they contain exactly the same elements, irrespective of the order or repetition.
options.B: Two sets are equal if they have at least one common element.
options.C: Two sets are equal if they have the same number of elements.
options.D: Two sets are equal if one is a subset of the other.

mcqs.answer: Two sets are equal if they contain exactly the same elements, irrespective of the order or repetition.
mcqs.explanation: Equal sets have precisely the same members; order and how the elements are written do not matter. Option A states this definition. Options B, C, and D describe different relationships (intersection, cardinality, and subset) that do not guarantee equality.

mcqs.question: Which pair of sets below are equivalent (i.e., have a one‑to‑one correspondence)?
mcqs.explanation: Two sets are equivalent when a bijection can be established between them, meaning they have the same cardinality. Set A has three elements each, so a one‑to‑one mapping exists. Options B and D have different numbers of elements, and while C is also equivalent (both empty), the question asks for a pair that clearly illustrates the concept; A is the best choice.

mcqs.question: What is the empty set?

options.A: A set that contains the number zero.
options.B: A set that contains no elements.
options.C: A set that contains only the element null.
options.D: A set that contains all natural numbers.

mcqs.answer: A set that contains no elements.
mcqs.explanation: The empty set, denoted by ∅ or {}, is defined as the set with no members at all. It is distinct from a set containing zero or null; those sets have one element each. Option B correctly captures the definition.

mcqs.question: Which of the following sets is a finite set?

options.B: The set of all prime numbers.
options.D: The set of all points on a line segment.

mcqs.explanation: A finite set contains a countable number of elements that can be listed completely. Option C has exactly four elements, making it finite. Options A, B, and D describe infinite collections.

mcqs.question: Identify the set that is infinite.
mcqs.explanation: An infinite set has no end; it contains endlessly many elements. The set of all natural numbers is unbounded, thus infinite. Options A and C are clearly finite, and D is the empty (finite) set.

mcqs.question: In a survey each participant selects exactly one favorite colour. The set containing the colour chosen by a particular participant is an example of which type of set?

options.C: Finite set with more than one element

mcqs.explanation: A singleton set contains exactly one element. Since each participant picks one colour, the set of that colour has a single member, making it a singleton. The other options describe sets with zero, multiple, or unlimited elements, which do not fit the scenario.

mcqs.question: Which statement about equal sets is FALSE?

options.A: Two sets are equal if they contain exactly the same elements, regardless of order.
options.B: Two sets are equal only if their elements are listed in the same sequence.
options.C: The empty set is equal to itself.

mcqs.answer: Two sets are equal only if their elements are listed in the same sequence.
mcqs.explanation: Equality of sets depends solely on membership, not on how elements are written. Therefore, statement B is false. Statements A, C, and D correctly describe the concept of equal sets.

mcqs.question: Which reasoning correctly demonstrates that the sets A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {a, b, c, d} are equivalent?

options.A: Both sets have four elements, so they are equivalent.
options.B: A bijection can be defined as f(1)=a, f(2)=b, f(3)=c, f(4)=d, establishing equivalence.
options.C: Since the elements are of different types, the sets cannot be equivalent.
options.D: They are equal because they have the same cardinality.

mcqs.answer: A bijection can be defined as f(1)=a, f(2)=b, f(3)=c, f(4)=d, establishing equivalence.
mcqs.explanation: Equivalence of sets is proved by exhibiting a one‑to‑one correspondence (bijection) between them. Option B explicitly provides such a mapping, satisfying the definition. Option A mentions cardinality but does not show the required bijection; Option C is incorrect because element type does not affect equivalence; Option D confuses equivalence with equality.
